Position: percentiles and quartiles

Percentile by hand (Anderson rule)Exam method
i=(p100)ni = \left(\frac{p}{100}\right) ni=(100p​)n

Step 2
if iii is not a whole number, round up: that position is the pppth percentile
Step 3

Counting, the rules of probability, random variables and the three named distributions. Topic pages: probability basics, conditional probability, random variables, distributions.

Rules of probability

Basic requirements and classical method
0≤P(Ei)≤1∑P(Ei)=1\begin{gathered} 0 \le P(E_i) \le 1 \\[5pt] \sum P(E_i) = 1 \end{gathered}0≤P(Ei​)≤1∑P(Ei​)=1​ P(A)=outcomes in Aequally likely outcomesP(A) = \frac{\text{outcomes in } A}{\text{equally likely outcomes}}P(A)=equally likely outcomesoutcomes in A​

Addition law
P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)\begin{aligned} P(A \cup B) &= P(A) + P(B) \\[5pt] &\quad - P(A \cap B) \end{aligned}P(A∪B)​=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)​

Conditional probability
P(A∣B)=P(A∩B)P(B),P(B)>0P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \quad P(B) \gt 0P(A∣B)=P(B)P(A∩B)​,P(B)>0

Use when

Multiplication law
P(A∩B)=P(B) P(A∣B)=P(A) P(B∣A)\begin{aligned} P(A \cap B) &= P(B)\,P(A \mid B) \\[5pt] &= P(A)\,P(B \mid A) \end{aligned}P(A∩B)​=P(B)P(A∣B)=P(A)P(B∣A)​

Independent events
P(A∣B)=P(A)⟺P(A∩B)=P(A) P(B)\begin{gathered} P(A \mid B) = P(A) \\[5pt] \Longleftrightarrow \\[5pt] P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B) \end{gathered}P(A∣B)=P(A)⟺P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)​
Test
compare P(A∩B)P(A \cap B)P(A∩B) with P(A)P(B)P(A)P(B)P(A)P(B); equal means independent
Careful

P(B)=∑j=1nP(Aj) P(B∣Aj)P(B) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} P(A_j)\,P(B \mid A_j)P(B)=j=1∑n​P(Aj​)P(B∣Aj​) P(Ai∣B)=P(Ai) P(B∣Ai)∑j=1nP(Aj) P(B∣Aj)P(A_i \mid B) = \frac{P(A_i)\,P(B \mid A_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} P(A_j)\,P(B \mid A_j)}P(Ai​∣B)=∑j=1n​P(Aj​)P(B∣Aj​)P(Ai​)P(B∣Ai​)​

All modules

Every Excel function in the course

In the table, r stands for a range such as B2:B51. Functions with a dot (STDEV.S, NORM.S.DIST) are the modern versions; the old ones (STDEV, NORMSDIST) still work but avoid mixing them.

FunctionReturnsExampleWatch out
Data preparation (Module 1)
COUNT / COUNTAnumber of numeric cells / non-empty cells=COUNT(r)COUNT skips text, so a gap between the two hints at numbers stored as text
COUNTBLANKnumber of empty cells=COUNTBLANK(r)quick missing-value check per column
COUNTIF / COUNTIFScount of cells meeting one / several conditions=COUNTIFS(A:A,"Delhi",C:C,">5000")builds frequency and contingency tables by hand
TRIMtext with extra spaces removed=TRIM(A2)"Delhi " and "Delhi" count as different categories until trimmed
IF + ISBLANKa flag or replacement for missing cells=IF(ISBLANK(B2),"missing",B2)decide and document how missing values are handled
RAND / RANDBETWEENrandom number in [0,1) / random whole number=RANDBETWEEN(1,500)recalculates on every edit; paste as values to freeze a sample
Descriptive statistics (Module 2)
AVERAGEarithmetic mean=AVERAGE(r)ignores blanks and text but counts zeros
AVERAGEIF / AVERAGEIFSmean of cells meeting conditions=AVERAGEIF(A:A,"Online",C:C)group means without a PivotTable
SUMPRODUCTsum of products of two ranges=SUMPRODUCT(w,x)/SUM(w)weighted mean, grouped mean, E(x), index numbers
MEDIANmiddle value=MEDIAN(r)
MODE.SNGL / MODE.MULTmost frequent value / all modes=MODE.SNGL(r)returns #N/A if no value repeats; SNGL shows only the first mode
GEOMEANgeometric mean=GEOMEAN(C2:C6)-1enter growth factors (1.08), not rates (8%)
TRIMMEANmean after dropping extremes=TRIMMEAN(r,0.1)0.1 drops 10% in total: 5% from each end
MIN / MAXsmallest / largest value=MAX(r)-MIN(r)range
LARGE / SMALLk-th largest / smallest value=LARGE(r,2)useful for sorted positions without sorting
QUARTILE.EXC / .INCQ1, Q2 or Q3=QUARTILE.EXC(r,3)EXC and INC use different position rules (see the table above); class files use EXC
PERCENTILE.EXC / .INCp-th percentile=PERCENTILE.EXC(r,0.9)p is a fraction (0.9), not 90
PERCENTRANK.INCpercentile rank of a value, as a fraction=PERCENTRANK.INC(r,B7)
RANK.AVG / RANK.EQrank of a value=RANK.AVG(B2,B$2:B$11,1)last argument 0 (default) ranks the largest as 1; 1 ranks the smallest as 1. RANK.AVG gives ties the average rank
VAR.S / VAR.Psample / population variance=VAR.S(r).S divides by n − 1, .P by N
STDEV.S / STDEV.Psample / population standard deviation=STDEV.S(r)use .S unless you truly have every member of the population
DEVSQsum of squared deviations from the mean=DEVSQ(r)gives SST in regression and ANOVA
SUMSQsum of squares of the values=SUMSQ(E2:E13)used for SSE and MSE of forecast errors
STANDARDIZEz-score=STANDARDIZE(B2,AVERAGE(r),STDEV.S(r))lock the ranges with $ before copying down
SKEW / SKEW.Psample / population skewness=SKEW(r)beyond ±1 means substantial skew
KURTexcess kurtosis=KURT(r)normal data give about 0 (not 3)
FREQUENCYcounts per bin=FREQUENCY(data,bins)returns one more cell than there are bins (values above the last bin)
Probability (Module 3)
FACTn!=FACT(5)
COMBIN / PERMUTcombinations / permutations of N taken n=COMBIN(10,3)COMBIN when order does not matter
BINOM.DISTbinomial P(X = x) or P(X ≤ x)=BINOM.DIST(3,10,0.3,FALSE)FALSE = exactly x; TRUE = x or fewer. "At least 3" is =1-BINOM.DIST(2,10,0.3,TRUE)
BINOM.DIST.RANGEP(x₁ ≤ X ≤ x₂)=BINOM.DIST.RANGE(10,0.3,2,4)note the argument order: n, p, then x values
POISSON.DISTPoisson P(X = x) or P(X ≤ x)=POISSON.DIST(2,4.5,FALSE)the mean must match the interval in the question
NORM.DISTnormal P(X ≤ x)=NORM.DIST(500,328,92,TRUE)always TRUE for probabilities; FALSE gives the curve's height, not a probability
NORM.S.DISTstandard normal P(Z ≤ z)=NORM.S.DIST(1.96,TRUE)the TRUE argument is required
NORM.INVx with a given area to its left=NORM.INV(0.9,328,92)"top 10%" means area 0.9 to the left
NORM.S.INVz with a given area to its left=NORM.S.INV(0.975)gives 1.96, the 95% two-tailed value
Inference (Module 3)
CONFIDENCE.NORMmargin of error with z=CONFIDENCE.NORM(0.05,sigma,n)returns the ± part only, not the interval; first argument is α, not 0.95
CONFIDENCE.Tmargin of error with t (df = n − 1)=CONFIDENCE.T(0.05,s,n)same warnings as CONFIDENCE.NORM
T.DISTleft-tail t probability=T.DIST(-2.1,24,TRUE)lower-tail p-value
T.DIST.RTright-tail t probability=T.DIST.RT(2.1,24)upper-tail p-value
T.DIST.2Ttwo-tailed t probability=T.DIST.2T(ABS(t),24)gives an error for negative t, so wrap it in ABS
T.INVt with a given area to its left=T.INV(0.95,24)one-tailed critical value
T.INV.2Ttwo-tailed critical t=T.INV.2T(0.05,24)enter α (0.05), and you get t0.025t_{0.025}t0.025​
Z.TESTp-value of a one-sample z test=Z.TEST(r,1056,1600)returns the one-tailed upper-tail p-value, P(Z ≥ z). Lower tail: =1-Z.TEST(…). Two-tailed: =2*MIN(Z.TEST(…),1-Z.TEST(…)). Leave σ out and it uses the sample SD
T.TESTp-value comparing two samples=T.TEST(A2:A21,B2:B21,2,1)tails = 1 or 2; type 1 = paired, 2 = equal variances, 3 = unequal. It never shows the t statistic. One-tailed results assume the difference is in the direction you observed
F.TESTtwo-tailed p-value for equal variances=F.TEST(A2:A21,B2:B21)a quick check before choosing T.TEST type 2 or 3
Relationships (Modules 2–4)
COVARIANCE.S / .Psample / population covariance=COVARIANCE.S(x,y)units are x-units × y-units, so hard to judge size
CORREL / PEARSONPearson r=CORREL(x,y)identical results
RSQr² of a simple regression=RSQ(y,x)
SLOPE / INTERCEPTb₁ / b₀=SLOPE(y,x)y range comes first
STEYXstandard error of the estimate, s=STEYX(y,x)y first again
LINESTarray of coefficients and fit statistics=LINEST(y,x1:x3,TRUE,TRUE)coefficients come out in reverse order (b3,b2,b1,b0b_3, b_2, b_1, b_0b3​,b2​,b1​,b0​); rows below give SEs, R² and s, F and df, SSR and SSE
TRENDfitted ŷ for new x values=TREND(y,x,new_x)works with several x columns

F.INV.RTcritical F=F.INV.RT(0.05,df1,df2)

CHISQ.INV.RTcritical χ²=CHISQ.INV.RT(0.05,2)

Decision rules and rules of thumb

Reject H₀ when…

One rule covers every test

Reject H0H_0H0​ if the p-value ≤α\le \alpha≤α. Otherwise "do not reject H0H_0H0​" (never "accept H1H_1H1​" without evidence, and never "prove H0H_0H0​").

Critical value approach (swap zzz for ttt with dfdfdf, as the test requires)
Form of H₁Reject H₀ ifp-value is
Lower tail, H1:μ<μ0H_1: \mu \lt \mu_0H1​:μ<μ0​z≤−zαz \le -z_{\alpha}z≤−zα​area to the left of the statistic
Upper tail, H1:μ>μ0H_1: \mu \gt \mu_0H1​:μ>μ0​z≥zαz \ge z_{\alpha}z≥zα​area to the right of the statistic
Two-tailed, H1:μ≠μ0H_1: \mu \ne \mu_0H1​:μ=μ0​z≤−zα/2z \le -z_{\alpha/2}z≤−zα/2​ or z≥zα/2z \ge z_{\alpha/2}z≥zα/2​2 × the area beyond ∣z∣|z|∣z∣
F test (ANOVA, regression), χ² teststatistic ≥\ge≥ critical valueright-tail area only
Most-used z values (the printed z-table gives 2.33 and 2.58 for the 0.01 and 0.005 tails)

Setting up H₀ and H₁

  • H0H_0H0​ always contains the equality: ===, ≤\le≤ or ≥\ge≥. H1H_1H1​ gets ≠\ne=, <\lt< or >\gt>.
  • The claim you want evidence for (the research hypothesis) goes in H1H_1H1​.
  • Testing someone else's claim ("at least 500 g per pack")? The claim sits in H0H_0H0​, and you look for evidence against it.
  • The direction of H1H_1H1​ decides the tail: <\lt< lower, >\gt> upper, ≠\ne= two-tailed.

Strength words for a correlation

A common rule of thumb; conventions vary, so always quote the number too
|r|Describe it as
0no linear relationship
below 0.3weak
0.3 to below 0.7moderate
0.7 to below 1strong
1perfect (all points on a straight line)

Add the direction: "a strong positive relationship (r = 0.82)". And remember that a strong r says nothing about cause.

Skewness

Excel SKEW valueShapeReport
between −0.5 and +0.5roughly symmetricmean and SD are fine
between ±0.5 and ±1moderately skewedgive the median alongside the mean
beyond ±1substantially skewedlead with the median and IQR

Positive = long right tail, mean above median. Negative = long left tail, mean below median.

Writing the conclusion (copy this shape)

  • Statistic and p-value: "t=−2.45t = -2.45t=−2.45, df=24df = 24df=24, p-value =0.011= 0.011=0.011."
  • Compare: "Since 0.011 ≤\le≤ 0.05, we reject H0H_0H0​."
  • Plain English, in context: "There is enough evidence at the 5% level that the average delivery time is below 30 minutes."
  • For a CI: "We are 95% confident that the mean basket value lies between ₹1,240 and ₹1,410."
